processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. EDS-measured composition of 15Al: Fe 44.6, Mn 35.2, Al 15.0, Cu 5.2 (at.%).
The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
After homogenization the ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.

processing_steps.method: solution treatment followed by oil quenching
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Samples (10 × 5 × 2 mm3) were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching. This is the parent process (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq) of the 525 °C/10 h aging. Solution-treated Vickers hardness of 15Al = 253.4 ± 2.1 HV.
The solution-treated 15Al sample was aged at 525 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching. This defines the terminal state of this sample (state label 525°C-10h).

structures.overall_structure: For the 15Al (Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu at.%) low-density steel after aging at 525 °C for 10 h, the microstructure is essentially a β-Mn matrix produced by the α→β-Mn transformation (the α matrix had been almost completely transformed into β-Mn within 3 h of aging at 525 °C), with fine new precipitates revealed within the β-Mn in the 10 μm SE inset. The transformation from the single-phase α (BCC) solution-treated state to the aged state produced a hardness rise from 253.4 HV to 915.7 HV.

phases_present.morphology: essentially featureless, uniformly transformed matrix at the 50 μm SE scale; β-Mn grows as short rod-shaped precipitates along α grain boundaries and inside α grains until they impinge and consume the matrix
fine precipitates distributed within the β-Mn (seen in the 10 μm inset of the 525 °C − 10 h SE panel)
fine precipitates distributed between/in the β-Mn

precipitates.distribution: within the β-Mn matrix (fine particles resolved only in the 10 μm SE inset)

interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase
interfaces.interface_notes: For the 15Al alloy at 525 °C the α matrix is almost completely transformed to β-Mn within 3 h (so the 10 h state is essentially fully β-Mn). The new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the β-Mn interfaces; the amount of FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content (so 15Al, the lowest-Al alloy, retains the largest amount of the ductile FCC Cu-rich phase).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured on an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample repeatedly tested 5 times and the hardness given by the average of 5 measurements. Samples were electrolytically polished with a mixture of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol before testing. Test temperature (room temperature) not explicitly stated.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N, dwell 15 s; 5 measurements per sample averaged; electrolytically polished samples
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the hardness of the 15Al alloy after the 525 °C/10 h aging treatment
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 15Al alloy aged at 525 °C for 10 h reached 915.7 ± 9.5 HV (compared with the solution-treated baseline of 253.4 ± 2.1 HV).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol); 50 μm main-field scale bar with 10 μm insets
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe the precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn, β-Mn, new precipitates) in the 15Al alloy after the different aging treatments including 525 °C for 10 h (Fig. 7)
characterization_methods.key_findings: At 525 °C − 10 h the SE image shows a featureless, uniformly transformed matrix with a 10 μm inset marked by magenta 'New precipitates' arrows; the α → β-Mn transformation proceeds fastest at higher aging temperatures.

unmapped_findings: For the 15Al alloy the elastic modulus E = 164 GPa (measured through compressive stress-strain curves) is reported and used in the indentation fracture-toughness equation (Eq. 1); this modulus is given for the 15Al alloy generally and is not reported specifically for the 525 °C/10 h sample.

The 15Al alloy aged at 525 °C for 10 h corresponds to the 10 h endpoint of the 525 °C series in Fig. 2; the 15Al hardness contour map shows a large >900 HV field covering most aging times above ~3 h and high temperatures, consistent with the 915.7 HV measured at 525 °C/10 h.

The specific hardness of 141 HV·cm3/g and the fracture toughness of 8.6 MPa·m1/2 for the 15Al alloy refer to its peak-hardness state (965.6 HV, achieved at 600 °C for 6 h), not to the 525 °C/10 h sample.

Neighbouring 15Al condition at 525 °C for 3 h (a different sample, not this one): a significant amount of β-Mn (85.8 %) had precipitated, hardness 872.0 ± 21.2 HV, with only a small amount of α matrix remaining.
